## A. Explore olympic_running data

This section introduces the olympic_running tsibble.

```r
olympic_running
olympic_running |> distinct(Length)
olympic_running$Year |> range()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Displays the olympic_running data.
- Shows unique lengths and year range.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The data covers different running lengths and years.
- Note the range of years.
:::

## B. Plot 100m times

Plot the 100m running times.

```r
olympic_running |>
  filter(Length=="100") |>
  autoplot(Time) +  
  geom_point()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters for 100m events.
- Plots time vs year with points.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Look for trends in running times.
- Note any missing observations.
:::

## C. Faceted plot of all lengths

Create a faceted plot for all lengths.

```r
olympic_running |>
  ggplot(aes(x=Year, y = Time, colour = Sex)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ Length, scales = "free_y", nrow = 2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_blank()) +
  labs(title = "Olympic running times",
       y="Seconds")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots times for all lengths, colored by sex.
- Uses facets for each length.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare trends across lengths and sexes.
- See how times have changed over years.
:::

## D. Summarise A10 costs

Summarise total A10 costs from PBS.

```r
a10 <- PBS |>
  filter(ATC2 == "A10") |>
  select(Month, Concession, Type, Cost) |>
  summarise(TotalC = sum(Cost)) |>
  mutate(Cost = TotalC / 1e6)

a10
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters PBS for A10 drugs.
- Sums costs across concession and type.
- Scales to millions.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The resulting tsibble has monthly data.
- Cost is now in millions.
:::

## E. Plot A10 costs

Plot the A10 cost time series.

```r
a10 |>
  autoplot(Cost) +
  labs(
    title = "Australian antidiabetic drug sales",
    y = "Cost $ (millions)"
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots the cost over time.
- Adds title and y-label.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Identify patterns: trend, seasonality, etc.
- This is a time series plot example.
:::

## F. Explore Snowy Mountains tourism

Filter and summarise Snowy Mountains data.

```r
snowy <- tourism |>
  filter(Region == "Snowy Mountains") |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips))
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters tourism for Snowy Mountains.
- Sums trips across purposes.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- This creates a quarterly series for the region.
:::

## G. Plot Snowy Mountains data

Use autoplot, gg_season, gg_subseries, ACF.

```r
snowy |> autoplot()
snowy |> gg_season()
snowy |> gg_subseries()
snowy |> ACF(Trips) |> autoplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Various plots: time plot, seasonal plot, subseries, ACF.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- What patterns do you learn from each plot?
- Seasonal effects, trends, autocorrelation.
:::

3.  You can compute and plot the daily changes in the Amazon stock price in 2018 using the code below. Do the daily changes look like white noise?

\fontsize{11.5}{15}\sf


```{r, eval = FALSE}
gafa_stock |>
  filter(Symbol == "AMZN", year(Date) >= 2018) |>
  mutate(trading_day = row_number()) |>
  update_tsibble(index=trading_day, regular=TRUE) |>
  mutate(diff = difference(Close)) |> 
  autoplot()

```

\fontsize{14}{16}\sf
